newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's high court backs labour flexibility-paper.
newsitem.headline: Spain's high court backs labour flexibility-paper.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court has upheld greater labour market flexibility by affirming less stringent criteria for layoffs, a local newspaper said on Friday.

The court, in an interpretation of a 1994 labour reform law, rejected the old standard whereby companies were justified in firing workers only if necessary for survival, the financial daily Expansion reported.
Court officials were not immediately available for comment.
The newspaper said the court ruled that companies could fire workers to overcome an economic crisis and no longer had to show the hardship was irreversible.

"These rulings are not trivial," Bank of America said in its daily commentary on Spanish markets. "They contribute significantly to making the implementation of the Labour Market Reform efficient by resolving a matter of definition which has blocked a long series of cases in the courts."
Spain has the highest unemployment in Europe and employers have long contended the cost of terminating permanent contracts is much higher than the European average.
Structural reforms, such as those in the labour market, are viewed as essential to improve Spain's competitive position in the run-up to European Monetary Union.

Spain's former Socialist government instituted labour reforms in an effort to ease rampant unemployment brought on by recession in 1992. Under the new Popular Party government, unions and employers are negotiating further reforms.
Candido Mendez, leader of one of Spain's largest unions UGT, decried the court ruling as a blow to workers.
"The labour reform allows firing of a worker at the going rate, opening up an unlimited number of justifications on the side of the company," Mendez said.
Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe General in Madrid, said the ruling was a successful test of labour reform law.
"The last barrier to firing has fallen...This creates a precedent in the Spanish legal system," he said.
